titulo.texto: Reconstruction of the Facade of the Temple of Quetzalcóatl

frase_gancho.texto: Feathered Serpents emerging from the sea where the world began.

puente_narrativo.texto: Follow the trail of water to a giant: the stone goddess who ruled over rivers and springs, so tall that you will have to lift your head to look her in the face.

guion_corto.texto: You are standing before a life-size replica of the facade of the Temple of the Feathered Serpent, one of the most sacred buildings in the Ciudadela of Teotihuacán, built around the year two hundred of our era. It is made of fiberglass and painted in the colors it once had: red, blue, sea green, and yellow. Notice the rhythm: serpent heads emerging from flowers, alternating with other heads with round eyes, and between them snail shells and seashells. For specialists, it is the sea from which the world was born. And beneath this temple, archaeologists found more than one hundred young people who had been sacrificed, wearing necklaces of jaws made of shell.

guion_largo.texto:
To imagine the place where this temple stood, think of the Ciudadela: a gigantic plaza, surrounded by platforms, with room for tens of thousands of people. The temple rose at the far end, painted red and other colors, like a stage set. What you see before you is a full-scale reproduction; the original facade, at the archaeological site, has lost almost all of its paint. Here you can see up close, and in full color, what a resident of the city saw.

Here is a surprising fact: “Quetzalcóatl” is a Mexica name, from a thousand years later. We do not know what the people of Teotihuacán called this serpent. What we do know is that the feathered serpent was already sacred here, long before the Toltec and the Mexica made it their own. In the Toltec Hall you will meet it again under the name Quetzalcóatl, and you will understand where its long fame comes from.

And why so many snail shells and seashells in the background? Because, according to several specialists, the facade represents the primordial sea, the water from which the world and time arise. The Feathered Serpents swim in that sea. The other heads, with round eyes and a headdress, are still debated: some read them as an earth monster linked to the calendar, others as a serpent of fire and war, and some find in them traits of Tláloc, the rain god you saw at the museum entrance.

This facade has reached us because it was covered up. Later, the people of Teotihuacán themselves built a platform in front of it, the Adosada Platform, which hid the front of the temple for centuries and protected it from rain, sun, and looting. Between 1917 and 1922, Manuel Gamio and his team explored the Ciudadela and brought to light part of that hidden facade. Without that platform, the reliefs would very likely have worn away until they vanished.

The most striking discovery lay underground. Around and beneath the temple, collective tombs appeared holding more than one hundred young people who had been sacrificed. Some had their hands tied behind their backs. Many wore necklaces made of shells carved to imitate human jaws. It is thought that they were warriors and that their death consecrated the building, as if the city had buried its military strength in the foundations of its most sacred temple.

And there is more. In 2003, after heavy rains, the entrance to a tunnel that had been sealed since antiquity was discovered, running beneath this temple. The INAH team exploring it has reported tens of thousands of objects and, in 2015, the presence of liquid mercury, a shining metal that, it has been proposed, made the tunnel look like an underground river of the underworld. Study continues today.

The facade also speaks of the world beyond the valley. The shells came from distant coasts, and the influence of Teotihuacán reached Maya territory: in Tikal, a hieroglyphic text tells that in the year three hundred seventy-eight a figure named Siyaj Kak, “Fire Is Born,” arrived, whom many specialists consider an envoy from Teotihuacán, and who soon afterward changed the local dynasty. You will reach that Maya world later on.

That is why this facade is much more than a decoration: it is a map of the cosmos, a message of power, and a tomb, all at the same time. As you move closer to the details, try not to see it as a museum replica, but as what it once was: the house of the serpent, in the plaza where the entire city gathered.

texto: Count the serpent heads you can see and notice the flowers they emerge from
Look for the snail shells and seashells in the background: they are the primordial sea
Look at the four colors of the facade and imagine that the whole city was this colorful

texto.Material: Full-size replica in fiberglass and polychrome pigments; the original building is made of carved stone, mortar, stucco and paint
texto.Origin: Teotihuacán, State of Mexico (the Citadel, Temple of Quetzalcóatl)
texto.Discovery: The original building was explored and identified between 1917 and 1922 by Manuel Gamio beneath the Attached Platform

texto.pregunta: Myth: Teotihuacán was always a gray city of bare stone.
texto.respuesta: Reality: It was painted red and many other colors; the stone we now see bare once had stucco and paint, like this facade.
